entry: Austrian-American actress and inventor. Born in [[Vienna]], Lamarr appeared in the controversial film *Ecstasy* (1933) in [[Czechoslovakia]] before becoming a Hollywood star with *Algiers* (1938). Her most successful film was *Samson and Delilah* (1949). She received a star on the [[Hollywood Walk of Fame]] in 1960. During [[World War II]], she and composer George Antheil co-invented a frequency-hopping radio guidance system for Allied [[Torpedo|torpedoes]], designed to resist jamming by the [[Axis powers]]. Similar technology entered operational use only in 1962.

Prefecture-level city (pop., 2020: 9,369,881), capital of Anhui province, [[China]]. Hefei is the political, economic and cultural center of Anhui and sits on a low saddle north of Chao Lake. The present city dates from the [[Song dynasty]]. Before [[World War II]] it was chiefly an administrative center and market for the fertile plain to the south. It is the site of the Experimental Advanced Superconducting Tokamak, a magnetic fusion reactor. Ranked 12th worldwide by the Nature Index in 2025, it is home to the University of Science and Technology of China and several other universities. It was the temporary capital of Anhui from 1853 to 1862.

Last division of classical Japanese history, 794–1185. Emperor Kammu moved the capital to Heian-kyō, modern [[Kyoto]], which remained the imperial capital for the next 1,000 years. Heian means "peace". Chinese influence declined and national culture matured. The syllabaries [[Katakana]] and [[Hiragana]] emerged, and court women wrote much of the vernacular literature. [[Murasaki Shikibu]]'s *The Tale of Genji* (c. 1000–1012) is often described as the world's first novel. Real power lay with the Fujiwara clan, which dominated the court through intermarriage with the imperial family. Warrior families, among them the [[Samurai|samurai]], grew in influence before the [[Shogun|shogunate]] was established in 1185.

Public research university in Heidelberg, [[Baden-Württemberg]], Germany. Founded in 1386 on the instruction of Pope Urban VI, it is Germany's oldest university and one of the world's oldest surviving universities. It was the third university established in the [[Holy Roman Empire]], after Prague (1347) and Vienna (1365). Modeled on the University of Paris, it originally had four faculties. It now has twelve faculties and offers degree programs in some 100 disciplines. Instruction is usually in German, though many graduate degrees are offered in English. Heidelberg students and faculty introduced modern scientific [[Psychiatry|psychiatry]], psychopharmacology and modern sociology as scientific disciplines. International students from some 130 countries make up more than 20 percent of the student body.

German-American model and television host. After winning a national modeling contest, Klum became a leading model and was the first German model to become a Victoria's Secret Angel. She hosted and judged *Project Runway* and *Germany's Next Topmodel*, and judged *America's Got Talent* on [[NBC]]. She shared a 2013 Emmy for hosting *Project Runway* and has been nominated for six Emmy Awards in total. In 2009 she became [[Barbie]]'s official ambassador. In 2011, [[Forbes]] estimated her total earnings for that year at US$20 million.

German poet and literary critic. Born in Düsseldorf into a Jewish family, Heine converted to Lutheran Christianity in 1825. He is best known outside Germany for early lyric poems that composers such as [[Felix Mendelssohn]], [[Robert Schumann]] and [[Franz Schubert]] set as *Lieder*. His later verse and prose are marked by satirical wit and irony. His radical political views led German authorities to ban many of his works, which only added to his fame. He spent the last 25 years of his life as an expatriate in Paris. Heine is remembered for the line "Where they burn books, they will ultimately burn people also," which ultimately came true in the [[The Holocaust|Holocaust]].

German physicist. Hertz was the first to conclusively prove the existence of the electromagnetic waves predicted by [[James Clerk Maxwell]]'s equations. He studied in Dresden, Munich and Berlin under [[Gustav Kirchhoff]] and [[Hermann von Helmholtz]], earning his doctorate in Berlin in 1880. At the University of Karlsruhe in 1886 he used spark-gap apparatus to produce and receive what are now called [[Radio wave|radio waves]], in the very high frequency range. In 1889 he became professor of physics at the University of Bonn, a post he held until his death. The SI unit of frequency, the hertz, is named in his honor.

German Nazi politician and police administrator. Himmler joined the [[Nazi Party]] in 1923 and the [[Schutzstaffel]] (SS) in 1925. He served as Reichsführer of the SS from 1929 to 1945, building it into one of the most powerful institutions in Nazi Germany. From 1943 he was both chief of the criminal police and minister of the interior, overseeing police and security forces, including the [[Gestapo]]. He was one of the main architects of the [[The Holocaust|Holocaust]], responsible for concentration and extermination camps and for the Einsatzgruppen death squads. He played a central role in the genocide of an estimated 5.5–6 million Jews. In April 1945 Hitler dismissed him after he attempted to open peace talks with the Western Allies. Captured by British forces, he committed [[Suicide|suicide]] in British custody.

German businessman and archaeologist. After a career in the import trade, Schliemann turned to archaeology. He was an advocate of the historicity of places in [[Homer]]'s epics. He excavated Hisarlık, presumed to be the site of [[Troy]], and the Mycenaean sites Mycenae and Tiryns. His work lent weight to the idea that the [[Iliad]] reflects historical events. Critics have argued that his excavation of nine layers of remains destroyed significant artifacts, including the layer believed to be Homeric Troy. Schliemann learned languages by keeping his diary in the language of whichever country he was in.

Historical region of the [[Arabian Peninsula]], now western [[Saudi Arabia]]. It includes the holy cities of [[Mecca]] and [[Medina]], the first and second holiest sites in [[Islam]]. Jeddah is its largest city, and the region is the most populated in Saudi Arabia. Hejazi Arabic is the most widely spoken dialect. According to Islamic tradition, Muhammad was born in Mecca. The area became part of the early Muslim conquests and of successive caliphates, first the [[Rashidun Caliphate]], then the [[Umayyad Caliphate]] and the [[Abbasid Caliphate]]. An independent Kingdom of Hejaz existed briefly in 1925 before it was conquered by the Sultanate of Nejd. In September 1932 the Kingdom of Hejaz and Nejd joined other Saudi territories to form the unified Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.

American actress. Hunt rose to fame as newlywed Jamie Buchman in the sitcom *Mad About You* (1992–1999), which earned her Golden Globe and Emmy awards. She won the Academy Award for Best Actress for *As Good as It Gets* (1997), playing a single mother opposite [[Jack Nicholson]]. Her films include *Twister* (1996), *Cast Away* (2000) and *Pay It Forward* (2000). She made her directorial debut with *Then She Found Me* (2007). Her family moved to [[New York City]] when she was three, and her father was a film and stage director.

American deafblind author and disability rights advocate. Keller lost her sight and hearing after an illness at 19 months old. At seven she met her teacher and lifelong companion Anne Sullivan, who taught her language. Keller attended Radcliffe College of [[Harvard University]] and became the first deafblind person in the United States to earn a college diploma. She wrote 14 books and hundreds of speeches and essays. Her autobiography, *The Story of My Life* (1903), described her education with Sullivan. Keller campaigned for disability rights, [[Women's suffrage|women's suffrage]], labor rights and [[World peace|world peace]]. She joined the Socialist Party of America in 1909 and was a founding member of the American Civil Liberties Union.

English actor. Mirren began with the National Youth Theatre and later joined the Royal Shakespeare Company. She won the Academy Award for Best Actress for *The Queen* (2006), playing [[Elizabeth II]]. She played the same monarch in the stage play *The Audience*, winning a Tony Award for it. On television she played DCI Jane Tennison in *Prime Suspect* (1991–2006), earning three British Academy Television Awards for Best Actress and two Primetime Emmy Awards. Her other films include *Excalibur* (1981) and *Red* (2010).

Figure in Greek mythology, said to be the most beautiful woman in the world. Helen was first married to Menelaus, king of [[Sparta]]. Her later marriage to Paris of [[Troy]] was the most immediate cause of the [[Trojan War]]. In most accounts, including [[Homer|Homer's]], she willingly went to Troy with Paris, though other stories describe an abduction. In Homer's account she was reunited with Menelaus after Paris died, but other versions have her ascend to Olympus. [[Christopher Marlowe]]'s *Doctor Faustus* (1604) contains the frequently cited line "Was this the face that launched a thousand ships."

Russian-American mystic and writer. Born into an aristocratic family in the [[Russian Empire]], Blavatsky co-founded the Theosophical Society in New York City in 1875 with Henry Steel Olcott and William Quan Judge. Her book *Isis Unveiled* (1877) outlined her worldview, which drew on [[Hermeticism]] and Neoplatonism. She described Theosophy as "the synthesis of science, religion and philosophy" and claimed it revived an ancient wisdom underlying all religions. The society moved to India in 1880. Critics accused Blavatsky of fraud, and a 1885 report by the Society for Psychical Research concluded that she had perpetrated fraud; the society questioned some of the report's methods in 1986. Supporters regarded her as an enlightened sage, and critics as a charlatan. She died of [[Influenza|influenza]]. Her doctrines influenced the spread of Hindu and Buddhist ideas in the West and the [[New Age|New Age Movement]].

Genus of around 50 species of flowering plants, the sunflowers. Helianthus belongs to the daisy family [[Asteraceae]] and is native to North America. The best-known species is the [[Common sunflower]] (*Helianthus annuus*), cultivated as a food crop for humans, cattle and poultry, and as an ornamental plant. The common sunflower is the national flower of [[Ukraine]], where it has been cultivated for several centuries. The wild sunflower is the state flower of [[Kansas]]. The whorled sunflower (*Helianthus verticillatus*) was listed as an endangered species in 2014, with its primary threats coming from pine plantations in Alabama, Georgia and Tennessee.

Gram-negative bacterium that infects the human [[Stomach|stomach]], often causing gastric ulcers and sometimes stomach cancer. *H. pylori* can cause [[Inflammation|inflammation]] of the stomach lining that becomes chronic gastritis. Most infected people have no symptoms. It was formally described in 1983 as the cause of gastric ulcers by Barry Marshall and Robin Warren, who received the 2005 Nobel Prize. It is classed as a Group 1 carcinogen. In 2023, about two-thirds of the world's population was estimated to be infected, with prevalence higher in developing countries.

Genus of 194 known species of flowering plants in the monotypic family Heliconiaceae. Most species are native to the tropical Americas, while a few grow on islands of the western Pacific and in Maluku, Indonesia. Common names include lobster-claws, toucan beak, wild plantain and false bird-of-paradise, the last reflecting resemblance to *Strelitzia*. Heliconias are the oldest known clade of [[Hummingbird|hummingbird]]-pollinated plants, originating in the Late Eocene (39 Ma). The genus was named by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in 1771. Most species are listed as vulnerable or data deficient by the IUCN Red List. Several are widely cultivated as ornamentals.

Type of rotorcraft in which horizontally spinning rotors supply lift and thrust. Helicopters can take off and land vertically, hover, and fly in any direction, so they operate where [[Fixed-wing aircraft|fixed-wing aircraft]] need a runway. The Focke-Wulf Fw 61 was the first successful, practical and fully controllable helicopter, in 1936. Igor Sikorsky's VS-300 became the basis for modern helicopters with a single main rotor and a tail rotor, the most common configuration. The Sikorsky R-4 was the first helicopter to reach full-scale production, in 1942. Quadcopters were pioneered in France as early as 1907, and multicopters are now widely used as [[Unmanned aerial vehicle|drones]]. The term was coined in 1861 by Gustave Ponton d'Amécourt.

Astrosphere of the [[Sun]], a bubble-shaped region of space. It is inflated by the outward flow of the [[Solar wind|solar wind]], which pushes back against the interstellar medium. The heliosphere shields the [[Solar System]] from much cosmic ionizing radiation, though uncharged gamma rays pass through. Its outer boundary, the heliopause, lies far beyond the orbit of Pluto. [[Voyager 1]] encountered the heliopause on 25 August 2012, and [[Voyager 2]] traversed it on 5 November 2018.

Light, stable [[Isotope|isotope]] of helium with two protons and one neutron. Its nucleus is called a helion. It contrasts with the more common helium-4, which has two neutrons. Helium-3 atoms are [[Fermion|fermions]] and become a superfluid at 2.491 mK. It was discovered in 1939. Helium-3 is thought to be more abundant on the [[Moon]] than on Earth, deposited there by the [[Solar wind|solar wind]] over billions of years. Its [[Nuclear fusion|nuclear fusion]] has long been viewed as a desirable energy source, because the fusion of two of its atoms would be aneutronic.

Chemical element with atomic number 2 and symbol He. It is a colorless, odorless, inert monatomic [[Noble gas|noble gas]] with the lowest boiling point of any element, and it has no melting point at standard pressures. Helium is the second-most abundant element in the observable universe, after [[Hydrogen]], and makes up about 24% of its elemental mass. It was first detected as an unknown yellow spectral line in sunlight in 1868, and isolated on Earth in 1895 by William Ramsay, Per Teodor Cleve and Nils Abraham Langlet. Cryogenics consumes about a quarter of production, and liquid helium cools the [[Superconductivity|superconducting]] magnets in MRI scanners. Helium also serves as a lifting gas in balloons and airships.

Place or state of posthumous punishment in many religions and folklore. Hell is usually located in another dimension or under the earth. Religions with a linear divine history, such as [[Christianity]], sometimes depict hell as eternal, while religions with [[Reincarnation|reincarnation]] usually depict it as an intermediary period between lives, as in the Indian religions such as [[Buddhism]]. Other traditions describe only an abode of the dead, such as [[Hades]]. As early as 1500 BCE, Egyptians asserted that the dead would be judged and punished. The [[Zoroastrianism|Zoroastrian]] concept of Duzakh is temporary and ends with the world's renovation.

Art of the Hellenistic period, roughly 323–30 BC. It is generally taken to begin with the death of [[Alexander the Great]] in 323 BC and to end with the Roman conquest of Ptolemaic [[Egypt]] after the Battle of Actium. It includes some of the best-known Greek sculpture, among them *Laocoön and His Sons*, the *Dying Gaul*, *Venus de Milo* and the *Winged Victory of Samothrace*. Royal patronage by the successor kingdoms fostered monumental architecture and sculpture. Some historians have described the style as decadent after the Golden Age of Classical Greece, though the terms [[Baroque]] and [[Rococo]] have also been applied to it.

Period of Greek and West Asian history, 323 to 30 BC. It began with the death of [[Alexander the Great]] and ended with the death of Cleopatra VII. After Alexander's conquests, Greek kingdoms were established in West Asia, including the [[Seleucid Empire]], in Northeast Africa, including the [[Ptolemaic Kingdom]], and in South Asia. Koine Greek became the [[Lingua franca|lingua franca]] of the region. Advances in mathematics by [[Euclid]] and [[Archimedes]] marked the era, and the philosophy of [[Stoicism]] emerged. The Roman conquest of Ptolemaic Egypt in 30 BC ended the last major Hellenistic kingdom, although scholars differ on the end date.
